Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Emotional outbursts will not solve student accommodation crisis – Vicky Bright Source : Emma Ankrah 21 November 2026 9:06am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
International corporate lawyer and entrepreneur Vicky Bright says emotional outbursts and public confrontations over university hostel fees will not resolve Ghana’s longstanding student accommodation crisis.
Her comments follow the ongoing disagreement between the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL) and the Rent Commissioner, Frederick Opoku, over proposed hostel fee increases, which has sparked concerns among students and parents about the affordability of university accommodation.
Speaking on JoyNews' Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mrs Bright argues that both university authorities and the Rent Commissioner have legitimate concerns, with universities seeking to recover the cost of providing accommodation while the Commissioner is concerned about affordability for students and their parents.
She said the debate must move beyond the disagreements and focus on finding sustainable solutions to the accommodation shortage.
“The shouting and all that, the emotional outbursts, those things are not going to resolve the problem...The university, on the one hand, has a credible case for recovering the cost of providing accommodation, and at the same time, the Rent Commissioner has a point because affordability is very important,” she said.
She added, “Banks are involved here, investors are involved here, and they are not charities. They are there. They've made investments, and somehow they have to recoup the initial capital plus make a return."
She maintained that the issue required a balanced approach that recognises the financial realities of universities and investors while protecting students and their families from unaffordable accommodation costs.
She noted that the crisis had developed over several years and had now reached a critical point, with some students forced to share rooms originally designed for one person.
On the proposed hostel fee adjustment, Mrs Bright acknowledged that the reduction from 26 per cent to 15 per cent was significant but said the revised increase would still place pressure on families.
She explained that the adjustment from about GH¢7,000 to GH¢8,050 would mean families paying more than GH¢1,000 in additional accommodation costs per term.
“For the families paying the bill, it's still another thousand-plus cedis a term,” she said.
Mrs Bright also questioned the quality of some university accommodation facilities, noting that the universities themselves had acknowledged that certain facilities were not fit for purpose.
